body:
Weekly Newsletter
                The New York art fairs, the worst of the Venice Biennale, Taryn Simon’s incomplete detective story, and Damien Hirst’s gay hole.  
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
    
        
            The following exchange between a curator and me takes place during the press preview for the Armory Show.  Me: “You look great!”Curator: “Thank you, I’ve been obsessed with money and lifting weights. How are you? It’s been a while.”  Me: “I’m okay, busy, you know ... Wait, did you say you’re ‘obsessed with money’?”Curator: “No, I said I’m obsessed with RUNNING.” On the way back to the office, I pass by the New Museum on the Lower East Side, which has just opened a major Arthur Jafa retrospective. A group of drug addicts is flailing in and out of consciousness just a few feet from the museum's sleek new glass expansion. One of them is rolling on the sidewalk in slow motion, wailing breathlessly, with an extinguished cigarette between his fingers. A second is piled on a stoop, waving away a fly that isn't there. A third is frozen in place, hunched over a dirty suitcase. Autumn winds are blowing, but the leaves have yet to fall from the trees. At this time of year, few things in the city are as beautiful as the Harlem River. The Manhattan skyline glimmers from behind a cemetery while the moon is split in half like a black-and-white cookie. A woman looks like she’s about to cry while reading Flannery O'Connor. A photographer is following a cute couple; they look back at the camera, smiling. A store is selling a jacket embroidered with the motivational message on the back, “Don’t be a little bitch.” “Would you like to try it on?” the woman behind the cash register asks. I say, “No, thanks. I’m just looking.”  — Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chiefArmory Week in New York

		This year’s edition seemed awfully quiet and downcast, making the financial sector trade show on the floor below seem like a riot in comparison. | Hakim Bishara

NewsA herd of 40 life-sized buffalo puppets migrated through parts of NYC this past weekend for Return of the Buffalo: Tatanka Owe Akupi (Lakota for “buffalo trail home”).Disgraced financier and MoMA board member Leon Black plans to convert an iconic Manhattan property into a foundation to display his estimated $5 billion art collection.Beijing-based artist Liu Wei returns to New York with brand-new works for the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Genesis Facade Commission. French authorities apprehend two German men at the Louvre Museum after they affixed two paintings to a wall in the room housing Leonardo da Vinci’s “Mona Lisa.”Christie’s launches a new pop culture division, with items for auction including music memorabilia, treasured instruments, and revered film props.Documenta 16 artistic director Naomi Beckwith says that some artists declined to participate in the exhibition over “Germany’s position on the Gaza war” and concerns about artistic freedom in the country.The Metropolitan Museum of Art will present the first major exhibition on Felix Gonzalez-Torres in New York in over 30 years.The El Museo del Barrio in New York expresses regret at providing rental space for a conspiracy-filled conference on the 25th anniversary of 9/11.A new report from the Joan Mitchell Foundation highlights deep structural issues affecting legacy work across the arts.Art Movements: Photographer Tyler Mitchell wins Crystal Bridges’s $250K prize, the National Gallery of Art names a new head of American Art, Sharif Bey wins the Spector Craft Prize, a Solange sculpture heads to the High Line, and more in Art Movements.From Our Critics

	
		
		The Worst National Pavilions at the Venice Biennale
		
	
	
		In the first part of this series, Editor-at-Large Hrag Vartanian and critic Aruna D’Souza discussed the pavilions they loved at the 61st Venice Biennale, running through November 22, and even made a provocative argument in favor of national pavilions. In this second and final installment, they take their gloves off to tear apart the pavilions they didn’t like and argue about the ones they’re split on. Brace yourself; it’s going to get heated. —Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief | Hrag Vartanian, Aruna D’Souza

		Tarot for a Broken World
		
	
	
		With some of the oldest surviving tarot decks on view, the Morgan’s exhibition traces how a Renaissance card game became something far more powerful. | AX Mina

		The Book of Alison Knowles
		
	
	
		A retrospective traces the language of bookmaking in her expansive work and its radical influence on American art. | Leah Triplett Harrington

title: “From Monet and Manet to Money”: A Berlin Museum Spotlights the Dealer Who Made Impressionism an International Sensation
description: Three women greet viewers to “Cassirer: Breakthrough of Impressionism” at Berlin’s Alte Nationalgalerie: Edgar Degas’s Miss La La (1879), Pierre-Aug
body:
Three women greet viewers to “Cassirer: Breakthrough of Impressionism” at Berlin’s Alte Nationalgalerie: Edgar Degas’s Miss La La (1879), Pierre-Auguste Renoir’s Lise with a Parasol (1867), and Max Slevogt’s 1901 portrait of Cassirer’s own daughter, Suzanne Aimée Cassirer. Two French, one German, all three paintings are connected to Paul Cassirer, the Berlin dealer who is credited with bringing Impressionism to Germany, including many works now in the Nationalgalerie collections; and with supporting German artists who furthered the developments of the avant-garde.Too often, we try to separate the art market from the museum, as if esteemed collections of now-canonical art could be held apart from the money with which they were bought and the circumstances in which they were sold. This exhibition and the accompanying catalog openly trace the mechanisms by which art crossed borders and exchanged hands. Impressionism ushered in a turn from art academies and state collections as arbiters of taste toward collectors and critics operating in a private market, making dealers essential to the eventual success of the movement. Lesser known than his French colleague and counterpart Paul Durand Ruel, Cassirer was the primary dealer of French Impressionism in Germany around the turn of the 20th century (Durand Ruel himself said Cassirer was exclusively responsible for bringing the group’s paintings across the Rhine).
	

	
		Related Articles
	



			
			
			
	
			
					Max Slevogt: Portrait Suzanne Aimée Cassirer, 1901.
									Oliver Ziebe, Berlin
	



	In the 19th century, French art predominated: This was both the advantage and the eventual controversy of Cassirer’s gallery. The dealer funneled foreign paintings to both private collectors and Berlin public collections at a time when the state was working to promote a German national style. Cassirer initially founded the Kunstsalon with his cousin Bruno in 1898, but the two soon split and Cassirer took over operations in 1901. Based in the fashionable Tiergarten district, Cassirer’s gallery had a sumptuous interior designed by the Art Nouveau architect Henry van de Velde. There, he displayed paintings in what were considered relatively spare, single row arrangements at a time when all-over salon-style hangs were in vogue.

	In addition to Degas and Renoir, Cassirer exhibited Monet, Manet, Cézanne, and van Gogh, as well as non-French artists including Edvard Munch. He did so for the love of art but also for profit: As a contemporary caricature of the gallerist quipped—“from Monet and Manet to money.” Cassirer was trained in art history and exhibited early Monet works, like the 1866 Jar of Peaches on view at the Alte Nationalgalerie, a painting that balances the restraint and containment of a glass jar of fruit with an expressively marbled tabletop. Shown at the same exhibition as the more radical Impression, Sunrise (1872), the inclusion of early still lives allowed Cassirer to construct a lineage for the movement that his patrons could follow. Manet’s great scandal, the 1863 Dejeuner sur l’herbe, was also shown at the Kunstsalon, though it did not find a buyer.
	


			
			
			
	
			
					View of the 2026 exhibition “Cassirer and the Breakthrough of Impressionism” at the Alte Nationalgalerie, Berlin.
									Photo David von Becker
	



	One of Cassirer’s strategies was to repeatedly exhibit unsold works as a way of acclimating the public to new styles, a strategy that resulted in what was then the largest ever exhibition of van Gogh in 1914, with 151 works. There are only 2 van Gogh works on view in the current exhibition at the Nationalgalerie, emphasizing a divide between what Cassirer showed and what the state wanted to collect. Van Gogh’s Boulevard de Clichy (1887), exhibited in 1905 and 1908 at Cassirer’s gallery, resonates with German Impressionist Curt Hermann’s Snow-Covered Roofs (1908/09), hung nearby. Both urban scenes are flecked with vivid color, an argument for the influence of French on German art.

	Mounting French influence was a problem for a cadre of German artists working to defend a conservative nationalist vision. In 1911, the landscape painter Carl Vinnen authored a “Protest by German Artists” against the influx of French work and gathered 140 signatures, to which Cassirer responded as part of a “Reply to a Protest by German Artists” organized by artists more sympathetic to internationalism, Wassily Kandinsky and Franz Marc. Already three years prior, the head of the Nationalgalerie, Hugo von Tschudi, had been ousted for his acquisition of French art via Cassirer as Kaiser Wilhelm II held an increasingly tight grasp on the national collections and preferred to promote German nationalism: This attempt to constrain museums to patriotic ends finds an uncomfortable echo in the US today, where museum exhibitions are increasingly under pressure from state priorities.
	


			
			
			
	
			
					Edgar Degas: Orchestra Musicians, 1872.
									©Städel Museum, Frankfurt am Main
	



	Cassirer’s story ended tragically, by suicide amid divorce proceedings. But his legacy for German art remains vividly present, not only in the works on view but in demonstrating the merit of greater transparency in the formation of museum collections and the motivations, spoken and unspoken, that shape them.

schema.headline: “From Monet and Manet to Money”: A Berlin Museum Spotlights the Dealer Who Made Impressionism an International Sensation
